rationale.conceptual: The method involves periodic DFT with a hybrid functional, geometry optimization, slab construction, and band-structure analysis. It is a standard protocol in computational materials science but requires careful parameter choice and understanding of surface termination effects, which elevates it above a simple textbook operation. Multiple interacting components (bulk, several slabs, modified surface energy formula) make it non-trivial.
rationale.execution: The pipeline includes bulk optimization, constructing five distinct slab models (different thicknesses and terminations), relaxing each, running band-structure calculations, extracting total energies and band gaps, and computing surface energies. This requires installing an open-source DFT code, handling pseudopotentials, and correctly setting up the (110) surface cells. It is a multi-stage workflow (~4-6 distinct stages) with dependencies, making it moderately complex orchestration.

difficulty.reasoning: The underlying paper applies standard periodic DFT with a hybrid functional (B3LYP) to a small unit cell material, to compute band gaps and surface energies. The conceptual difficulty is moderate (established multi-part method requiring careful implementation but no novel algorithm). The execution requires constructing several slab models, running multiple DFT calculations, and applying a modified surface energy formula; a multi-stage pipeline but not excessively long or fragile. Resource needs are very light, no GPU required.

compute_estimate.reasoning: The calculations involve small unit cells (up to 18 atoms) using hybrid DFT, which is CPU-bound. The reference solution estimates 7-8 hours of CPU time. A few GB of RAM suffices; no large datasets beyond tiny crystal structures and pseudopotentials.
